lens: Fact and integrity audit of /home/user/livewell-land/client/public/essays/why-does-god-feel-far-away.json (updated 2026-10-28) against its claims ledger /home/user/livewell-land/docs/work/essays/ledgers/why-does-god-feel-far-away.md, the BSB and STEPBible Hebrew in /home/user/livewell-land/client/public/bible/ch/, a local ESV 2011 copy (lguenth/mdbible commit fd66568, json/ESV.json, in the session scratchpad at src/mdbible/json/ESV.json), and the integrity rules in /home/user/Livewell-/docs/work/essays/BRIEF.md. Read-only on the essay and ledger. The published body is identical to docs/work/essays/why-does-god-feel-far-away.md apart from the title and standfirst lines, and scripts/validate-essays.mjs reports 'Essays: clean (15 files)'. Every sentence was read for checkable claims; every quotation, number, date, name, title and attribution was matched to a ledger line. All 18 Scripture quotation strings were re-compared by script with the ESV copy this run and all match. This run used 8 of its 30 web searches on 2026-10-28 and saw search-engine summaries only: content.time.com failed in WebFetch (host not resolvable in this session) and curl got CONNECT 403, so no page was opened. No claim is wrong as printed. The findings are two restorations that sources now support, one loose paraphrase of Taylor, one Scripture quotation without its own reference, and three small ledger gaps.

findings.where: What the Church Called the Dark Night, Mother Teresa paragraph: "They showed that for decades, through most of the years she spent among the poor and dying of Calcutta, she felt almost nothing of God's presence."
findings.problem: (g) Restoration. The ledger's 'Dropped by the writer on 2026-10-26' list records the writer's original, more specific claim that her darkness lasted "nearly fifty years, from around 1949", and ledger section 2 already records the closing pass seeing Time's 2007 story by David Van Biema: "for the last nearly half-century of her life she felt no presence of God whatsoever". This run's searches saw the same span again: Time's "for the last nearly half-century" (via an albertmohler.com result discussing the Time piece); America magazine's 2007 review of Come Be My Light (americamagazine.org, "My soul's long dark night"), which put the aridity at roughly 50 years with one brief respite until her death in September 1997; a Come Be My Light book listing saying "for nearly fifty years until her death"; and a Project MUSE article ("Behold a Pale Horse") saying almost fifty years. One outlier, Christian Century, said "some 45 years", which still fits "nearly fifty" loosely. No source this run or earlier confirmed the start year 1949, so the year stays out.
findings.fix: Replace "They showed that for decades, through most of the years she spent among the poor and dying of Calcutta, she felt almost nothing of God's presence." with "They showed that for nearly fifty years, through most of the years she spent among the poor and dying of Calcutta, she felt almost nothing of God's presence." Do not restore "from around 1949". In the ledger, move the line out of the dropped list and add it under section 2 with these sources (Time/Van Biema 2007; America 2007 review; the book listing; Project MUSE), noting the Christian Century 45-year figure.

findings.where: Lament in the Psalms, first paragraph: "The Psalter is full of laments, and many of them are addressed to a God who seems to have left the room."
findings.problem: (g) Restoration. Correction 7 changed the writer's original "Dozens of psalms are laments" to "The Psalter is full of laments" only because no source for the count had been seen. This run's search saw three: John F. Fink's column in The Criterion (archindy.org, 12 March 2010), saying sixty-three psalms are classified as laments (forty-five individual, eighteen community); a Working Preacher commentary on Psalm 22 (workingpreacher.org), saying over one-third of the Psalms are laments; and Claus Westermann, quoted in a CUHK theology publication, putting the individual laments alone at about 50 of the 150. Counts differ by classification, but every one is in the dozens, so "dozens" is now supported and is the more specific wording.
findings.fix: Replace "The Psalter is full of laments, and many of them are addressed to a God who seems to have left the room." with "Dozens of psalms are laments, and many of them are addressed to a God who seems to have left the room." In the ledger, mark correction 7 as restored, citing Fink (63; 45 individual, 18 community), Working Preacher (over a third) and Westermann (about 50 individual laments), all as search summaries.

findings.where: The Age We Live In, first paragraph: "Meaning lived out in the world, in relics and holy places and the turning of the seasons, and it acted on them whether they chose it or not."
findings.problem: (c) The ledger's own line for this paraphrase (section 1, Taylor, last bullet) calls it "the softest detail" and says "no source used the word seasons". The source that line rests on, the Gifford Archives summary, describes medieval life lived within "the ebb and flow of higher and ordinary times", which is the sacred calendar. This run's two Taylor searches saw the same and nothing about seasons: the giffordarchives.org summary of medieval life moving between higher and ordinary times, with Carnival breaking up the religious calendar, and a Wikipedia summary of A Secular Age saying the enchanted world took God, sacraments, relics and sacred places to have real effects. "The turning of the seasons" reads as the natural or farming year, and the sentence credits it to Taylor's account. Relics and holy places are supported. The seasons are not.
findings.fix: Replace "in relics and holy places and the turning of the seasons," with "in relics and holy places and the feast days of the church year,". The sentence becomes: "Meaning lived out in the world, in relics and holy places and the feast days of the church year, and it acted on them whether they chose it or not." Update the ledger's "turning of the seasons" bullet to match.

findings.where: The Argument from Hiddenness, last paragraph: "When Paul stood before the philosophers of Athens, in a city with an altar inscribed "To the unknown god," he told them God had made the nations "that they should seek God, ..." (Acts 17:27)."
findings.problem: (e) "To the unknown god" is verbatim ESV Scripture in quotation marks (Acts 17:23; ledger section 3 line; matched again this run in the ESV copy: "I found also an altar with this inscription, To the unknown god."; BSB: "TO AN UNKNOWN GOD"). The only reference near it is Acts 17:27, which belongs to the next quotation, so a reader checking the inscription would look in the wrong verse. BRIEF.md asks for the reference beside each Scripture quotation.
findings.fix: Change "in a city with an altar inscribed "To the unknown god," he told them" to "in a city with an altar inscribed "To the unknown god" (Acts 17:23), he told them". Nothing else in the sentence changes.

findings.where: The Argument from Hiddenness, last paragraph: "The word "perhaps" is in Paul's own sentence, and he knew what groping in the dark was."
findings.problem: (a) A claim about Paul's own experience with no ledger line, and nothing in the essay grounds it. It is probably meant to recall Acts 9:8-9 (ESV copy: "although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus. And for three days he was without sight"; BSB: same sense). As printed, the reader is given an unsupported biographical aside.
findings.fix: Either keep the text and add a ledger line tying it to Acts 9:8-9 (ESV copy and BSB), or make the tie explicit: "The word "perhaps" is in Paul's own sentence, and he had once been led by the hand into Damascus, unable to see (Acts 9:8)." If neither, cut the clause: "The word "perhaps" is in Paul's own sentence."

findings.where: Lament in the Psalms, first paragraph: "In the Psalter they're a prayer, written for worship and sung by Israel and the church ever since."
findings.problem: (a) The ledger supports "written for worship" (Psalm 13 is headed "To the choirmaster"; ESV copy and BSB), but it has no line for "sung by Israel and the church ever since". The claim is general and sound (the Psalter's temple headings, and the church's continuous use of the psalms in its worship), but it is untraced.
findings.fix: No text change needed. Add a ledger line recording it as a general statement grounded in the Psalter's liturgical headings (for example Psalm 13 and Psalm 88, "To the choirmaster", ESV copy and BSB) and the church's psalmody. If the fixer prefers the narrower claim, use "written for worship and prayed by Israel and the church ever since."

findings.where: The Age We Live In, first paragraph: "He calls the older self porous." and "Taylor calls the modern self buffered."
findings.problem: (g) Optional restoration and a ledger correction. Correction 8 removed the quotation marks from the writer's original 'He calls the older self "porous."' and 'Taylor calls the modern self "buffered."' because the words could not then be matched. The final pass afterwards confirmed by search that "the porous self" and "the buffered self" are Taylor's own terms, and this run's Taylor search saw the same (americamagazine.org, traditiononline.org). Correction 8's rationale also says the approved pilot what-post-christian-means names Taylor's "subtraction stories" without quotation marks. The live pilot (client/public/essays/what-post-christian-means.json) in fact reads 'Taylor also refused what he called "subtraction stories,"', with marks, though it leaves cross-pressured unmarked. Both forms are accurate, so this is a choice, not an error.
findings.fix: Optional: restore 'He calls the older self "porous."' and 'Taylor calls the modern self "buffered."' Either way, correct the ledger's correction-8 note so it no longer says the pilot leaves "subtraction stories" unquoted.

John of the Cross: Carmelite reform under Teresa of Avila; seized December 1577 and taken to the priory in Toledo; about nine months (Teresa's own figure in Letter 260); 'could hardly fit' as paraphrase; poetry in the cell; escape August 1578; poem then later commentary (correction 3); 'dark night of the soul' as the English title phrase; Dark Night I.9's other causes of dryness (sins, lukewarmness, bodily humours). All match the ledger and Peers.
